evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Positive pressure layer jamming allows compressive pressure on jamming layers to exceed atmospheric limits, delivering approximately 1.6 times higher payload capacity than low-cost vacuum equivalent levels.

Multi-material additive manufacturing combining PETG and TPU enables monolithic printing of rigid constraint frames, strain-limiting layers, and airtight bellows, reducing post-processing and manual assembly.
The soft gripper achieved approximately a 25-fold stiffness variation with positive layer jamming, maintaining a constant slope without distinct slip across a 6 mm deflection at 45 psi.
Pull-out force increased with jamming pressure and reached a saturation plateau around 35 psi with an average force of 80 N, exceeding vacuum-equivalent thresholds.
Inter-layer stiction caused erratic hysteresis at lower jamming pressures, but residual deformation dropped to near zero at 35 psi and above as layers remained locked in the pre-slip regime.

Inverting actuation by employing a constant-force spring for closing and pneumatic bellows for straightening places the jamming layers in tension along the inner radius during payload loading, avoiding layer buckling.
At 45 psi, the gripper exhibited an average opening time of 0.24 s, a closing time of 0.29 s, and a tip position repeatability standard deviation of 0.13 mm.
A two-finger gripper integrated as an end-effector on an industrial UR5 robot arm successfully manipulated items weighing up to 1.7 kg when positive layer jamming was engaged.

experimental_setup: Stiffness testing: Single finger clamped to a rigid base in its naturally curved state; deflected by 6 mm and unloaded over 5 trials per pressure level using a force sensor on a motorized linear stage.

Pull-out force testing: Dual-finger gripper mounted on a base grasping a cardboard tube linked by cord to a force gauge on a linear stage; stage retracted until full pull-out occurred across 5 trials per pressure level.

Actuation evaluation: Tip position repeatability measured before and after cycling at 45 psi via force sensor and linear stage; opening pressure evaluated incrementally up to 45 psi; opening and closing durations captured at 45 psi using slow-motion video and solenoid valve control.

Robotic manipulation: Dual-finger gripper installed as an end-effector on a Universal Robots UR5 manipulator, controlled through UR5 software and solenoid valves to perform pick-and-place tasks with objects ranging from 0.1 kg to 1.7 kg.
future_work: Design and evaluate an isolated positive pressure jamming link independent of an actuator to characterize and optimize stiffness change without grip force interference (Page 6).
Investigate varying geometrical and material parameters such as jamming channel dimensions, layer counts, and substrate materials (Page 6).
Incorporate positive pressure layer jamming into conventional forward-actuated gripper configurations to overcome the grip force limits of spring-driven closing (Page 6).
Enhance the robustness of multi-material additive manufacturing for more intricate internal geometries (Page 6).
Conduct systematic fatigue life and endurance characterization of 3D-printed TPU/PETG pneumatic actuators (Page 6).
Further analyze and model inter-layer stiction, friction, and hysteresis behaviors across operating pressures (Page 4).

limitations_inferred: Because pull-out force saturates around 35 psi once layer slipping is suppressed (Phase 1 pre-slip), maximum payload becomes constrained by the structural and flexural compliance of the PETG/TPU gripper rather than jamming pressure.

The positive pressure layer jamming mechanism requires a rigid external constraint frame and an inflatable pressure bag, adding geometric bulk and localized rigidity compared to flexible vacuum envelopes.
The experimental study only evaluated a single layer thickness (0.13 mm), one layer material (Mylar), and an 11-segment geometry, leaving parameter sensitivity unverified.
Wear, surface degradation, and long-term hermetic sealing integrity of 3D-printed interfaces and sliding Mylar layers under repeated positive pressure cycles were not evaluated.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Stiffness change was measured in the curved grasping posture where spring grip force contributed to baseline stiffness, preventing direct comparison with planar vacuum layer jamming compliant links (Page 6).
The inverted spring-driven design relies on a 3.7 N spring, resulting in relatively low closing grip strength and restricting graspable payload forms (Pages 2, 6).

FDM 3D-printed TPU actuators have considerably lower fatigue life than molded silicone actuators (85A TPU actuators failed at 600 cycles vs. 10^6 cycles for 28A silicone in referenced studies) (Page 4, 6).

Additive manufacturing of soft elastomers requires specialized extrusion hardware, low print speeds, and is limited to commercially available hardness levels (softest ~60A FDM vs. ~10A for casting silicones) (Page 4).
Hysteresis was inconsistent at lower jamming pressures due to unpredictable stiction between layers (Page 4).
Higher standard deviation in pull-out force at elevated pressures was attributed to unpredictable slip between layers and slip against the cardboard object (Page 5).
Slight assembly variations introduced uneven internal friction, causing different fingers to require slightly different pressures to fully open (Page 5).
main_results: The positive pressure layer jamming soft gripper demonstrated an approximately 25-fold variation in stiffness between the unjammed state and full positive pressure jamming.
Jamming at 45 psi (310.3 kPa) prevented inter-layer slip throughout the 6 mm deflection range and increased average stiffness by 1.85 N/mm over vacuum-equivalent jamming at 14.7 psi (101.4 kPa).

Dual-finger pull-out force increased with jamming pressure and saturated at 35 psi (241.3 kPa) at an average peak force of 80 N, representing a 1.6-fold increase over 12.5 psi low-cost vacuum and a 1.16-fold increase over 14.7 psi atmospheric pressure.
Residual deformation (hysteresis) dropped to near zero at 35 psi and above as the Mylar sheets remained locked in the pre-slip regime (Phase 1).
Actuation was rapid (opening time 0.24 s, closing time 0.29 s at 45 psi) with high tip repeatability (standard deviation of 0.13 mm).
The gripper integrated on a UR5 industrial robot arm successfully grasped and manipulated various items up to 1.7 kg.
performance_metrics: Stiffness variation factor (~25x overall stiffness increase; 13x at 12.5 psi)
Average stiffness increase over vacuum-equivalent pressure (1.85 N/mm increase at 45 psi vs. 14.7 psi)
Peak pull-out force (80 N average at 35-45 psi, 1.6x higher than 12.5 psi and 1.16x higher than 14.7 psi)
Opening time (0.24 s) and closing time (0.29 s) at 45 psi
Gripper tip repeatability standard deviation (0.13 mm)
Tested pressure limit (up to 60 psi / 413.7 kPa)
Maximum payload lifted in robot trials (1.7 kg)
possible_gap_implications: While positive pressure layer jamming removes the atmospheric pressure ceiling inherent to vacuum jamming, the requirement for a rigid reaction frame increases mechanical complexity and segment rigidity, presenting an unexplored trade-off between soft robotic compliance and load capacity.

The saturation of payload capacity in Phase 1 suggests that merely increasing pressure yields diminishing returns; future designs must optimize structural bending stiffness, constraint frame modulus, and layer friction coefficients rather than pneumatic pressure alone.

Overcoming the low grip force caused by inverted spring actuation requires developing positive pressure jamming architectures that can be incorporated directly into forward-actuated bending fingers without inducing compressive layer buckling.
paper.research_objective: To design, multi-material 3D-print, and experimentally evaluate a soft robotic gripper with tunable stiffness enabled by a novel positive pressure layer jamming mechanism capable of exceeding the pressure limits and payload capacity of traditional vacuum-based jamming.
paper.research_problem: Soft robotic grippers possess inherent compliance and simplified control but suffer from low payload capacity. Existing variable-stiffness layer jamming technologies rely predominantly on vacuum compression inside an airtight envelope, which is fundamentally limited by atmospheric pressure (14.7 psi / 101.4 kPa), restricting maximum joint stiffness and holding force.
paper.title: A 3D Printed Soft Robotic Gripper With a Variable Stiffness Enabled by a Novel Positive Pressure Layer Jamming Technology
